title: Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance - CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance - The Evaluation Blackout Period
subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: The period during an active procurement in which all communications between potential bidders and agency staff/evaluators are strictly restricted is commonly known as:
options: The Cone of Silence
The FOIA Window
The Due Diligence Phase
The Estoppel Period
questions.explain: The 'Cone of Silence' or blackout period is a rule designed to prevent undue influence. It restricts communications between vendors and government officials during the solicitation and evaluation phase.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: During a blackout period (Cone of Silence), how are vendors typically required to communicate their technical questions about the solicitation to the agency?
options: By calling the mayor or city council directly.
By directly emailing the subject matter experts on the evaluation committee.
By submitting questions in writing solely to the designated procurement officer.
Vendors are not allowed to ask any questions once a solicitation is published.
questions.explain: To ensure fairness and consistency of information, all inquiries during the blackout period must be funneled in writing through a single point of contact, usually the designated procurement officer, who then issues an addendum to all.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: When does the 'Cone of Silence' typically end in a public procurement cycle?
options: Immediately after the bids are opened.
When the highest-ranked vendor gives their oral presentation.
Upon the formal award of the contract or the issuance of a Notice of Intent to Award.
It never ends; vendor communication remains restricted indefinitely.
questions.explain: The blackout period ends when the decision-making process is complete, which is usually signaled by a formal Notice of Intent to Award or the final approval of the contract by the governing body.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: An evaluator accidentally runs into a representative of a bidding vendor at a local grocery store during the active blackout period. The vendor begins discussing their pending proposal. What is the evaluator's legal and ethical obligation?
options: Listen politely but offer no response.
Immediately stop the conversation, explain the blackout period, and report the encounter to the procurement officer.
Allow the vendor to talk, but write down everything they say for the other evaluators.
Tell the vendor that their proposal is currently in last place.
questions.explain: To maintain integrity, the evaluator must immediately halt the improper communication, remind the vendor of the blackout rules, and notify procurement so the incident is documented and addressed.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: During an RFP blackout period, Vendor A wishes to clarify a confusing technical specification. What is the standard procedural mechanism the agency uses to ensure Vendor A receives the answer without violating the blackout rules?
options: The buyer calls Vendor A privately.
The buyer requires Vendor A to guess.
The buyer collects Vendor A's written question, then publishes the question and answer in a formal Addendum available to all potential bidders.
The buyer tells Vendor A to submit a separate bid covering both interpretations.
questions.explain: The proper mechanism is issuing an addendum. This addresses the vendor's question in writing and ensures all competing vendors have access to the exact same information simultaneously, preserving fairness.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: Under typical 'Cone of Silence' regulations, which of the following communications is permitted during an active solicitation phase?
options: A vendor emailing the Mayor to complain about the specifications.
A vendor asking an evaluator for a status update at a networking event.
A vendor publicly speaking during the allotted open question time at a mandatory pre-bid conference.
A vendor taking a city council member to lunch to discuss community needs.
questions.explain: Formal public meetings, such as pre-bid conferences, public bid openings, or recorded evaluation presentations, are explicit exceptions to the Cone of Silence, provided the communication occurs openly in the formal, structured environment.
